name: La Louisianne Records and Studio
writeup: Carol Rachou sold records and phonographs in Lafayette from 1954 and, by his own account to historian Shane Bernard, opened this studio in 1958 in a former grocery store. His La Louisianne label followed in 1959, named for its first release, "Sud de la Louisiane." Cajun bandleaders such as Aldus Roger and Nathan Abshire recorded for him, and so did swamp pop acts including the Shondells. Dale and Grace's "I'm Leaving It Up to You," issued on Sam Montel's Montel label, was cut here and reached number one nationally in late 1963. Rachou's son David now runs the studio.

name: Central Louisiana State Hospital Cemetery (Amédé Ardoin's burial place)
writeup: Amédé Ardoin, the Creole accordionist and singer whose early 1930s records with fiddler Dennis McGee shaped both Creole and Cajun music, ended his life far from the prairies where he played. After a beating that followed a dance around 1939, his health and mind failed. He was admitted to the state hospital at Pineville on September 26, 1942, and died there on November 3. He lies somewhere on this hillside among more than two thousand patients whose graves carry no names, only a few numbered markers. A historical marker stands at the cemetery; his statue is in St. Landry Parish.

name: Bois Sec Ardoin's grave, Ceaser Cemetery
writeup: Alphonse "Bois Sec" Ardoin was born in 1915 near Bayou Duralde, in a Creole farming settlement between Mamou and Basile, and never moved far from it. From 1948 he and fiddler Canray Fontenot played house dances as the Duralde Ramblers, keeping the old accordion and fiddle la-la alive; they appeared at the Newport Folk Festival in 1966 and were both named National Heritage Fellows in 1986. His son Morris ran Club Morris nearby, where the family band played. Ardoin died on May 16, 2007, and was buried in this country cemetery, which is why the point is dated from 2007.

name: Clifton Chenier's grave, All Saints Cemetery
writeup: Clifton Chenier, born in Opelousas in 1925, made some of the first zydeco records in 1954, signed with Specialty in 1955 and spent the next three decades carrying the piano accordion and his Red Hot Louisiana Band across the country and overseas. In 1984 he won a Grammy and a National Heritage Fellowship. He died in Lafayette on December 12, 1987. After a packed funeral mass there a week later, at which his son C.J. played his accordion, the King of Zydeco was buried in this cemetery outside Loreauville, on the Bayou Teche side of Iberia Parish.

name: Peaches Records, Gentilly Boulevard (former store)
writeup: Shirani Rea's record shop opened on Gentilly Boulevard by 1984; it is mapped here from 1991, when bounce began and the store became its main counter. A Times-Picayune writer called it the epicenter of the bounce craze, reporting that local bounce tapes outsold national rap stars there ten to one. Mia X worked the register from 1990 and sold thousands of copies of her own answer record, "Da Payback." Master P and the Cash Money owners dealt with Rea directly, and Mannie Fresh tried out new tracks on her customers. The store flooded after Hurricane Katrina; Peaches now trades on Magazine Street.
sources: A Closer Walk (Ponderosa Stomp Foundation and WWOZ), Peaches Records <https://acloserwalknola.com/places/peaches-records/>

name: Odyssey Records, Carrollton Shopping Center (site)
writeup: Henry Holzenthal and his sons opened Odyssey Records here in 1980 and moved into a larger storefront in the same strip mall in 1986, the year this point begins. Gary Holzenthal stocked turntables and mixers and welcomed rap when other white retailers avoided it, so the city's DJs gathered here. DJ Khaled worked behind the counter, as did Leroy "Precise" Edwards, who produced DJ Jimi's bounce hit "Where They At." In 1993, at an autograph session, eleven-year-old Lil Wayne rapped for Cash Money co-founder Bryan "Baby" Williams. Odyssey left for Canal Street in 2002; a Costco parking lot covers the site.

name: The Nite Cap (site)
writeup: This corner of Louisiana Avenue and Carondelet Street held a nightclub from 1946, whites-only at first under other names. In 1967 it became the Nite Cap, and Art Neville put together a band there with his brothers Aaron and Cyril and a young rhythm section: Zigaboo Modeliste, George Porter Jr. and Leo Nocentelli. Those four left for a small bandstand at the Ivanhoe on Bourbon Street and became the Meters, who later rehearsed Fire on the Bayou here. In 1977 the newly formed Neville Brothers were announced to make their debut at the club. The building burned in 2014 and the lot is empty.

name: Tuba Fats Square
writeup: One evening in 2007, brass band musicians led mourners through Tremé to play for Kerwin James, a tuba player who had just died. Police answering a noise complaint sent more than twenty cars and took Derrick Tabb and Glen David Andrews away in handcuffs. Many saw it as an attack on a neighborhood custom generations old. In response the owner of this corner lot at St. Philip and North Robertson, with Tremé musicians, named it for Anthony "Tuba Fats" Lacen, the bandleader who taught so many young players, and set it aside for music. A Tuba Fats Tuesday festival has been held here since 2009.

name: A.L. Davis Park (Shakespeare Park) and Uptown Super Sunday
writeup: Central City's park at Washington Avenue and LaSalle Street, dedicated to Mayor Joseph Shakspeare in 1900 and renamed for the Rev. A.L. Davis in 1979, was a gathering place for Black New Orleanians shut out of other parks. Michael P. Smith photographed the Wild Magnolias performing here at a benefit about 1974, the date used for this point. Each spring it is home to Uptown Super Sunday, when Mardi Gras Indian tribes walk the neighborhood in their new suits and DJ Jubilee emcees the stage. Chief Howard Miller of the Creole Wild West taught children beading here, and second lines pass its corner.
